# Block affine normalization and an explicit dense-lattice depth bound

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): proved sufficient condition, with an explicit feasible point.
This note uses the uniform closed-cap discrepancy proved in
`candidate 0639bd50a01557c4` and the
classical continuous Grünbaum inequality. It does not assume mixed OC.
Every convex body admits the block normalization below; the small
covering-radius condition is an additional hypothesis, not something
the normalization automatically supplies.

Write

    Gamma_0=1,   Gamma_k=(k/(k+1))^k  (k>=1),
    kappa_k=vol_k(B_2^k),   kappa_0=1.

All depths are normalized by the indicated measure's total mass.
The main result concerns n>=1,d>=0,N=n+d>=1. In positive continuous
dimension its mesh hypothesis itself ensures positive d-dimensional
fiber measure; thus no lower-dimensional original fibers are silently
treated as full-dimensional ones.

## 1. An elementary normalization preserving the vertical subspace

Let C be any compact convex body in R^n times R^d. There is an
invertible affine map

    F(z,x)=(A z+t, B z+T x+c),                             (1)

with A in GL_n and T in GL_d, such that, for

    R=N(N+2),   K=F(C),

one has

    B_2^N subset K subset R B_2^N.                         (2)

For d=0 the T determinant and the continuous Jacobian below mean one.

Here is a direct construction. Choose a maximum-volume inscribed
N-simplex in C; a positive maximum exists by compactness. Map its
vertices affinely to 0,e_1,...,e_N, obtaining C'. If lambda_i(x) are
the barycentric coordinates of any x in C', replacement of the i-th
simplex vertex by x changes the volume by the factor |lambda_i(x)|.
Maximality therefore gives |lambda_i(x)|<=1 for every i. In particular
each ordinary coordinate x_i=lambda_i(x), i>=1, belongs to [-1,1], so

    Delta=conv(0,e_1,...,e_N) subset C' subset [-1,1]^N.

The centroid g_Delta=(1,...,1)/(N+1) has distance 1/(N+1) from each
coordinate facet and distance

    r_N=1/((N+1)sqrt(N))

from the remaining facet. Consequently translation by -g_Delta and
dilation by r_N^(-1) put a unit ball inside the image. The enclosing
radius is at most

    sqrt(N) (N+2)/(N+1) / r_N = N(N+2)=R.

Let L_0 be the linear part of this preliminary normalization. Its image
W=L_0({0} times R^d) is a d-dimensional linear subspace. Choose an
orthogonal transformation O taking W onto the standard vertical
subspace {0} times R^d. This preserves both balls in (2). The linear
part O L_0 takes the vertical subspace onto itself, so its upper-right
block is zero. Its restrictions to that subspace and to the quotient
are invertible. This is exactly the block form (1).

No compatibility, smoothness, symmetry, or lattice-aligned simplex is
needed. The orthogonal transformation is applied after the preliminary
normalization; it need not preserve the original integer lattice.

## 2. The transformed lattice and the exact measure factor

Under (1),

    F(Z^n times R^d)=(A Z^n+t) times R^d.

Put L=A Z^n, v_L=|det A|, and let delta be its Euclidean covering
radius. The coset translation t does not change delta. Define on K

    nu(E)=v_L sum_(lambda in L+t) vol_d((K intersect E)_lambda).
                                                               (3)

For the original full-fiber measure

    mu(E)=sum_(z in Z^n) vol_d((C intersect E)_z),

the fiber map x -> Bz+Tx+c has the SAME Jacobian |det T| at every z.
Hence, for every Borel set E,

    nu(F(E))=|det A| |det T| mu(E)=|det DF| mu(E).          (4)

In this formula E may be intersected with C on either side. For d=0
both fiber measures are counting measures on singleton fibers, and
(4) still holds with |det T|=1. Thus normalized cap masses and depths
are exactly invariant. Although Bz depends on z, it is a translation
on each fiber and contributes no additional Jacobian.

A Voronoi cell for L, with its boundary assigned measurably among
adjacent cells, lies in B_2^n(delta), hence in [-delta,delta]^n.
The closed-cap discrepancy in the cited sampling note therefore gives,
with V=vol_N(K),

    |nu(K)-V| <= epsilon(delta),
    |nu(H)-vol_N(K intersect H)| <= epsilon(delta)
                         for EVERY closed halfspace H,             (5)

where

    epsilon(delta)=2n delta(2R+2delta)^(N-1).

The notation nu(H) already includes restriction to K. In particular,
(5) retains sampled boundary fibers and also covers d=0.

## 3. Quantitative centroid interiority and base-only rounding

Let g be the ordinary N-dimensional centroid of K. Then

    g+R^(-N) B_2^N subset K.                              (6)

Indeed, for a unit vector v and h=h_K(v), (2) gives h>=1 and

    h-v dot g
      = V^(-1) integral_K (h-v dot y) dy
      >= V^(-1) integral_(B_2^N) (h-v dot y) dy
      = kappa_N h/V
      >= R^(-N),

because the integrand is nonnegative on K and V<=kappa_N R^N.
Taking all support directions proves (6).

Choose a nearest point lambda in L+t to the base coordinates g_z,
and set

    y=(lambda,g_x).                                      (7)

Then |y-g|<=delta. If delta<=R^(-N)/2, (6) shows that y is in int K.
In particular its own d-fiber is full dimensional when d>=1, and
nu(K)>0. When d=0, y itself is a sampled point, so nu(K)>0 as well.
The inverse image F^(-1)y is an actual mixed-integer point of int C.

Set

    S_N=kappa_(N-1) R^(N-1).

Every hyperplane section of K has (N-1)-volume at most S_N, since it
lies in a section of R B_2^N. For N=1 this states that a nonempty
zero-dimensional section has counting measure one. Moving the
threshold of a unit-normal halfspace by distance at most delta loses
at most S_N delta in ordinary volume, by Fubini. Continuous Grünbaum
at g consequently gives, for every closed H containing y,

    vol_N(K intersect H) >= Gamma_N V-S_N delta.           (8)

To see that this includes every such H, first shrink it to the parallel
halfspace through y, then compare with the parallel halfspace through
g. Ordinary hyperplane volume is zero, so this comparison has no
ordinary-volume boundary correction; the sampled boundary correction
is already retained in (5).

Combining (5) and (8), for every alpha>=0,

    nu(H)-alpha nu(K)
       >= (Gamma_N-alpha)V-S_N delta
                            -(1+alpha)epsilon(delta).    (9)

This inequality, rather than a quotient approximation with a possibly
negative numerator, will be used below.

## 4. An explicit sufficient mesh size for the exact target

Suppose

    alpha=2^(-n) Gamma_d < Gamma_N.

Define

    E_(n,N)=2n(2R+2)^(N-1),

    delta_*(n,d)=min {
        1/(2R^N),
        (Gamma_N-alpha)kappa_N /
                   [S_N+(1+alpha)E_(n,N)]
    }.                                                   (10)

**Theorem.** If the block normalization (1)--(2) has transformed
base-lattice covering radius delta<=delta_*(n,d), then the explicit
point F^(-1)(lambda,g_x), with lambda nearest to g_z, has original
mixed depth at least

    2^(-n) Gamma_d.                                       (11)

Proof: the first part of (10) ensures feasibility and positive total
mass by Section 3. It also gives delta<=1. Thus
epsilon(delta)<=E_(n,N)delta. Since V>=kappa_N, the second part of
(10) makes the right side of (9) nonnegative for every closed cap.
Divide by nu(K)>0 and apply the exact invariance (4).

The strict inequality required for (10) holds for EVERY n>=1,d>=1,
and also for d=0,n>=2. One elementary verification is
Gamma_k<=1/2 for k>=1, by the first two terms of the binomial expansion,
and Gamma_k>1/3 because

    (1+1/k)^k <= sum_(j=0)^k 1/j! < 3.

In the first case alpha<=1/4; in the second alpha<=1/4 as well.

A version not involving unit-ball volumes follows from
kappa_N>=(2/sqrt(N))^N and kappa_(N-1)<=2^(N-1). Since alpha<=1/4
in all these cases, the stronger, more restrictive condition

    delta <= min {
        1/(2R^N),
        (Gamma_N-alpha)(2/sqrt(N))^N /
                       [(1+3n)(2R+2)^(N-1)]
    }                                                    (12)

also suffices. The constants are deliberately elementary; no
optimality is claimed.

The proof is uniform in ALL bodies satisfying (2), all lattice cosets,
and all closed caps. It therefore gives an actual uniform dense-regime
bound, stronger than merely taking a fixed body's limiting depth.
It does not assert that every normalized lattice has such a small
covering radius.

## 5. One integer coordinate: a projection-length criterion

Now n=1,d>=1, and write

    W=max_(C) z-min_(C) z

for the original projection length, measured in the original integer
coordinate. In (1) the base map is z -> a z+t. The transformed
projection length is |a| W, and (2) bounds it by 2R. The transformed
one-dimensional lattice has spacing |a| and covering radius |a|/2.
Therefore, for EVERY block normalization constructed above,

    delta=|a|/2 <= R/W.                                   (13)

Consequently

    W >= R/delta_*(1,d)                                  (14)

is a sufficient condition for the exact original bound Gamma_d/2,
with the point again given by base-only rounding after normalization.
There is no assumption on the position of the projection interval
relative to Z: its coset is already included in (5).

For example, when n=d=1, N=2,R=8,

    Gamma_2-alpha=7/36,   S_2=16,   E_(1,2)=36,
    delta_*(1,1)=min{1/128, 7 pi/2196}=1/128.

The last equality follows already from pi>3. Thus projection length
W>=1024 is an explicit, nonoptimal sufficient bound in that case.
This example illustrates the constants; it is not claimed as the
sharp interval-fiber theorem.

For n>1, the comparable datum here is the covering radius of A Z^n.
A claim replacing it by an arbitrary single projection width or by
an unproved lattice splitting is not part of the result.

## 6. Degenerate-dimensional conventions and scope

* For n=1,d=0, Gamma_1=Gamma_0/2 and the gap in (10) is zero. Every
  finite nonempty sampled interval nevertheless has a median lattice
  point of depth at least 1/2. This is a direct counting argument,
  independent of discrepancy. The normalization exists, but (10) is
  not used to extract an exact bound from a zero gap.
* For n=0,d>=1, ordinary Grünbaum gives Gamma_d directly; there is no
  base rounding or transformed lattice condition. The case n=d=0 is
  excluded, as in the task; no depth convention for an infimum over
  an empty set of nonzero ambient normals is introduced here.
* If d>=1 but the original mixed set initially has only lower-dimensional
  nonempty fibers, its full d-fiber measure is zero. Such a body cannot
  satisfy the sufficient mesh condition: (6)--(7) would produce an
  interior mixed point and therefore a positive d-fiber. The theorem
  does not assign d-volume to those lower-dimensional fibers.
* The original ambient C is full dimensional. The condition is a
  genuine dense-lattice regime of the full-dimensional problem; it
  does not remove the separate intrinsic-dimension reductions needed
  for arbitrary mixed sets or prove OC outside that regime.

The dependency chain is: maximum inscribed simplex -> block affine
normalization and exact measure factor -> continuous centroid
interiority and Grünbaum -> uniform closed-cap lattice discrepancy ->
the explicit inequality (9). No extraction, cap-selector, conditional
mixed-centroid, or unproved induction lemma is used.
